e-6168.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Definite Integral of an Exponential Function
e-6168.worked_solution:
Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={e}^{x}{|}_{0}^{5} \\  & ={e}^{5}-{e}^{0} \\  & ={e}^{5}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

e-412.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Definite Integral of a Trigonometric Function
e-412.worked_solution:
Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: An antiderivative of 10^x is 10^x/ln(10). Evaluating from 0 to 2 gives (100-1)/ln(10)=99/ln(10), so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{10}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{10}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}\cdot {10}^{x}\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}({10}^{2}-{10}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}(100-1) \\  & =\frac{99}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}.\end{aligned}
$$
